desc:
A chess knight stands on cell (sr, sc) of an empty n x n board (rows and columns are numbered from 0). One move changes the position by (±1, ±2) or (±2, ±1) and must stay on the board. The knight may visit the same cell any number of times.

Return the number of different sequences of exactly k moves that finish on cell (tr, tc), modulo 1,000,000,007. Two sequences differ when their lists of visited cells differ.

n = 3, k = 2, from (0,0) to (0,0)  ->  2
n = 3, k = 2, from (0,0) to (2,2)  ->  0
n = 3, k = 1, from (0,0) to (1,2)  ->  1
hints: Do not try to enumerate the walks: there are up to 8<sup>k</sup> of them. How many different (cell, moves left) situations are there instead?
Let f[t][r][c] be the number of t-move walks from the start that end at (r, c).
Push each cell's count to the up to 8 cells a knight reaches from it to build layer t+1 from layer t, starting from a single 1 on the start cell. Read the answer from layer k at the target.
editorial: A walk of t+1 moves is a walk of t moves followed by one more knight move. So if f[t] holds the number of t-move walks ending at each cell, then f[t+1][b] is the sum of f[t][a] over all cells a from which a knight move reaches b. Equivalently, push the count of every cell to its up to 8 knight neighbours. Layer 0 contains a single 1 on the start cell.

After k layers, the answer is f[k][tr][tc]. Each layer costs 8 · n2 operations, so the total is O(k · n2) time and O(n2) space. Counts are reduced modulo 1,000,000,007 per layer. A parity fact gives quick sanity checks: every knight move flips the colour of the square, so if k is odd the target must have the opposite colour to the start, otherwise the answer is 0.
